# Setup

1.2 1.2

Using the tibble created earlier, find the Ozone amount when the temperature was 97. Show this by both subsetting the entire row and pinpointing the Ozone element only. Also, for both ways, use Base R approach as well as Tidyverse approach.

# Base R: show the entire row where Temp equals 97.
air.tib[air.tib$Temp == 97, ] 
# A tibble: 1 × 6
  Ozone Solar.R  Wind  Temp Month   Day
  <int>   <int> <dbl> <int> <int> <int>
1    76     203   9.7    97     8    28
# Base R: show only the Ozone value where Temp equals 97.
air.tib[air.tib$Temp == 97, "Ozone"] 
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  Ozone
  <int>
1    76
# Tidyverse: show the entire row where Temp equals 97.
air.tib |> filter(Temp == 97) 
# A tibble: 1 × 6
  Ozone Solar.R  Wind  Temp Month   Day
  <int>   <int> <dbl> <int> <int> <int>
1    76     203   9.7    97     8    28
# Tidyverse: show only the Ozone value where Temp equals 97.
air.tib |> filter(Temp == 97) |> select(Ozone)
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  Ozone
  <int>
1    76

2 Ex 2

Use the flights data for this exercise.

2.1 2.1

Select only the top 10 worst arrival delays for each day for each month for each year. Using the subset of the data, calculate the average delay for each month regardless of the dates or years.

# Group by year, month, and day first. 
# Then select the 10 worst arrival delays for each day.
worst_daily_delays <- flights |> 
  filter(!is.na(arr_delay)) |> group_by(year, month, day) |> 
  slice_max(order_by = arr_delay, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |> 
  ungroup()

# Print the subset to confirm it worked.
worst_daily_delays
# A tibble: 3,650 × 19
    year month   day dep_time sched_dep_time dep_delay arr_time sched_arr_time
   <int> <int> <int>    <int>          <int>     <dbl>    <int>          <int>
 1  2013     1     1      848           1835       853     1001           1950
 2  2013     1     1     2343           1724       379      314           1938
 3  2013     1     1     1815           1325       290     2120           1542
 4  2013     1     1     1842           1422       260     1958           1535
 5  2013     1     1     2115           1700       255     2330           1920
 6  2013     1     1     2205           1720       285       46           2040
 7  2013     1     1     2006           1630       216     2230           1848
 8  2013     1     1     2312           2000       192       21           2110
 9  2013     1     1     1942           1705       157     2124           1830
10  2013     1     1     1938           1703       155     2109           1823
# ℹ 3,640 more rows
# ℹ 11 more variables: arr_delay <dbl>, carrier <chr>, flight <int>,
#   tailnum <chr>, origin <chr>, dest <chr>, air_time <dbl>, distance <dbl>,
#   hour <dbl>, minute <dbl>, time_hour <dttm>
# Calculate the average of those worst delays by month.
monthly_worst_delay_avg <- worst_daily_delays |> 
  group_by(month) |> 
  summarize( 
    avg_arr_delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop" 
    ) 

# Print the monthly summary. 
monthly_worst_delay_avg

2.2 2.2

Visualize the data that shows average delays each month. Style the chart appropriately to make the chart presentable.

monthly_worst_delay_avg |>
  mutate(month = factor(month, levels = 1:12, labels = month.name)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = avg_arr_delay)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  labs( 
    title = "Average of the Top 10 Worst Arrival Delays by Month", 
    subtitle = "Based on the worst 10 arrival delays for each day", 
    x = "Month", 
    y = "Average arrival delay in minutes", 
    caption = "Data source: nycflights13 flights dataset"
  ) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), 
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold") 
  )

2.3 2.3

Describe what you learned from the data about delays.

Note


It looks like some months have much higher delays than others. Summer and winter seem to have the biggest delays, although this chart by itself doesn’t explain exactly why.

The final goal of this exercise is to visualize the data. To do so, I first need to understand the data and then reshape it into a format that works better for visualization.

The relig_income data set is a tibble with 18 rows and 11 variables. Each row represents a religion category, and the columns after religion represent different income brackets. I don’tt see missing values in the data from the missing value check.

3.2 3.2

Look up the help documentation for relig_income.

# Open the help documentation for the data set.
help(relig_income)

The help documentation explains that relig_income contains counts based on religion and income categories. The religion column identifies the religious group, and the other columns represent income ranges. The values in those income columns are counts. This helped me understand that the numbers are frequencies, not actual income amounts for individual people.

3.3 3.3

Think about the relationships among the variables you want to visualize. One potential idea is to show what the frequency of income brackets looks like by religion. Does the current data allow you to support your goal? Why or why not? If the data does not support the goal, how should the data be reshaped?

The current data gives the information needed, but it is not in the best shape for the visualization yet. The income brackets are stored as column names instead of being values in one income column. Because of that, the data is wider than it needs to be. To make it tidy, each row should represent one religion and one income bracket, with the count in a separate column. Reshaping the data into a longer format makes it easier to use ggplot() because income can become one variable and count can become another variable.

3.4 3.4

Reshape the data. Draw a plot that shows income distribution by religion.

# Reshape the data from wide to long format.
relig_income_longer <- relig_income |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -religion,
    names_to = "income",
    values_to = "count"
  ) |>
  filter(income != "Don't know/refused")

# Print the reshaped data to confirm it worked.
relig_income_longer
# A tibble: 162 × 3
   religion income    count
   <chr>    <chr>     <dbl>
 1 Agnostic <$10k        27
 2 Agnostic $10-20k      34
 3 Agnostic $20-30k      60
 4 Agnostic $30-40k      81
 5 Agnostic $40-50k      76
 6 Agnostic $50-75k     137
 7 Agnostic $75-100k    122
 8 Agnostic $100-150k   109
 9 Agnostic >150k        84
10 Atheist  <$10k        12
# ℹ 152 more rows
# Create a plot showing income distribution by religion.
relig_income_longer |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, y = count)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ religion, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Income Distribution by Religion",
    subtitle = "Counts are shown across income brackets for each religion group",
    x = "Income bracket",
    y = "Count",
    caption = "Data source: tidyr relig_income dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

The reshaped version is much easier to graph because income is now one column instead of several separate columns. I used facets so each religion has its own small chart. This makes the chart easier to read than trying to put every religion into one crowded graph.

3.5 3.5

Redo 3.4 using one long chain of code from the first step to the last.

relig_income |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -religion,
    names_to = "income",
    values_to = "count"
  ) |>
  filter(income != "Don't know/refused") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, y = count)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ religion, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Income Distribution by Religion",
    subtitle = "This version uses one chained tidyverse workflow",
    x = "Income bracket",
    y = "Count",
    caption = "Data source: tidyr relig_income dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

The us_rent_income data set has rent and income information by state. It has five variables: GEOID, NAME, variable, estimate, and moe. The variable column separates income and rent, while the estimate column contains the values. Based on the missing value check, there are no missing values.

4.2 4.2

Type code that will show the description of the data in the help documentation. Then read the description of the variables.

# Open the help documentation for this data set.
help(us_rent_income)

The help page explains that this data comes from the American Community Survey. GEOID is the geographic ID, and NAME is the state name. The variable column shows whether the row is about income or rent. The estimate column gives the estimated value, and moe is the margin of error.

4.3 4.3

Think about the relationship between income and rent across the states. Does the current data shape support the visualization goal? Why or why not?

The current data has the information needed, but it is not shaped in the easiest way for a scatterplot. Right now, income and rent are both stored in the variable column, so they are not separate columns yet. To graph the relationship between income and rent, each state should have one row with separate income and rent columns. Reshaping the data wider makes the relationship much easier to visualize.

4.4 4.4

Reshape the data. Draw a plot that shows the relationship between income and rent across the states.

# Reshape the data so income and rent become separate columns.
us_rent_income_wider <- us_rent_income |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = variable,
    values_from = c(estimate, moe)
  )

# Print the reshaped data to confirm it worked.
us_rent_income_wider
# A tibble: 52 × 6
   GEOID NAME                 estimate_income estimate_rent moe_income moe_rent
   <chr> <chr>                          <dbl>         <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>
 1 01    Alabama                        24476           747        136        3
 2 02    Alaska                         32940          1200        508       13
 3 04    Arizona                        27517           972        148        4
 4 05    Arkansas                       23789           709        165        5
 5 06    California                     29454          1358        109        3
 6 08    Colorado                       32401          1125        109        5
 7 09    Connecticut                    35326          1123        195        5
 8 10    Delaware                       31560          1076        247       10

10 12    Florida                        25952          1077         70        3
# ℹ 42 more rows
# Visualize the relationship between income and rent.
us_rent_income_wider |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate_income, y = estimate_rent)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Income and Rent by State",
    subtitle = "Each point represents one state",
    x = "Median income estimate",
    y = "Median rent estimate",
    caption = "Data source: tidyr us_rent_income dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

The scatterplot suggests a positive relationship between income and rent. States with higher median income also tend to have higher median rent. This makes sense because places with higher incomes often have higher housing costs too. I would still describe this as an association, not proof that one variable causes the other.

Run the code below.

mba <- data.frame(
  player = c("A", "A", "B", "B", "C", "C"),
  year = c(1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2),
  stats = c("22/2/3", "29/3/4", "18/6/7", "11/1/2", "12/1/1", "19/2/4")
)

mba

5.1 5.1

Separate the number of the stats column into points, assists, and steals. Assign this data frame to a new name, mba_sep. Print out the data set.

# Separate the stats column into three columns.
mba_sep <- mba |>
  separate(
    col = stats,
    into = c("points", "assists", "steals"),
    sep = "/",
    convert = TRUE
  )

# Print the separated data.
mba_sep

5.2 5.2

Reverse the last question by uniting three columns: points, assists, and steals, into one column. Assign mba_uni to the data frame. Then confirm the work by printing it out.

# Unite the three stat columns back into one column.

  unite(

6 Ex 6

Use the flights data.

6.1 6.1

Filter the data by including only the flights that were not canceled. For each day, calculate the first and last departure times from NYC airport. Then, for each month, select one day such that the first flight departure was the latest for the month. Show the results in descending order of first_dep in a table using gt.

# Keep only flights that have a departure time.
# These are treated as flights that were not canceled.
daily_departures <- flights |>
  filter(!is.na(dep_time)) |>
  group_by(year, month, day) |>
  summarize(
    first_dep = min(dep_time),
    last_dep = max(dep_time),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Print the daily summary to confirm it worked.
daily_departures

The finding makes sense because the busiest routes from New York airports are usually connected to major cities and common travel destinations. 7 Ex 7

Using the data frame air.tib, find out how many missing values exist in the column Solar.R and what percent of the record the missing values account for. Next, create a variable called Solar_Mean and assign the mean of the column Solar.R to it. Finally, replace all the missing values in Solar.R with Solar_Mean. Confirm that there are no more missing values in this column.

# Count missing values in Solar.R and calculate the percent missing.
solar_missing_summary <- air.tib |>
  summarize(
    missing_values = sum(is.na(Solar.R)),
    total_records = n(),
    percent_missing = missing_values / total_records * 100
  )

# Print the missing value summary.
solar_missing_summary
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  missing_values total_records percent_missing
           <int>         <int>           <dbl>
1              7           153            4.58
# Calculate the mean of Solar.R while ignoring missing values.
Solar_Mean <- mean(air.tib$Solar.R, na.rm = TRUE)

# Print the mean to confirm it worked.
Solar_Mean
[1] 185.9315
# Replace missing Solar.R values with the mean.
air.tib <- air.tib |>
  mutate(
    Solar.R = if_else(is.na(Solar.R), Solar_Mean, Solar.R)
  )

# Confirm that there are no more missing values in Solar.R.
air.tib |>
  summarize(
    missing_values_after = sum(is.na(Solar.R))
  )
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  missing_values_after
                 <int>
1                    0

air.tib

8 Ex 8

Use the air.tib data frame. The goal is to visualize the monthly total temperature with a barplot with Month on the y-axis and total temperature on the x-axis. Do the appropriate wrangling and visualization in one chain of code.

air.tib |>
  count(Month, wt = Temp) |>
  mutate(
    Month = case_when(
      Month == 5 ~ "May",
      Month == 6 ~ "June",
      Month == 7 ~ "July",
      Month == 8 ~ "August",
      Month == 9 ~ "September"
    ),
    Month = factor(Month),
    Month = fct_reorder(Month, n, .desc = FALSE)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = Month)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Total Monthly Temperature",
    subtitle = "Month is ordered by total temperature",
    x = "Total temperature",
    y = "Month",
    caption = "Data source: airquality dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

The chart shows the total temperature for each month after grouping and summarizing the data. July and August had the highest totals, which matches what I expected. This exercise helped me understand how multiple tidyverse functions can work together in a single pipeline.

9 Ex 9

Using the air.tib data frame, group the data set by Month. Next, find out the maximum temperature for each month and display the result. Then, pipe the wrangled data into ggplot() and draw an appropriate chart.

# Find the maximum temperature for each month.
monthly_max_temp <- air.tib |>
  group_by(Month) |>
  summarize(
    max_temp = max(Temp),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Month = case_when(
      Month == 5 ~ "May",
      Month == 6 ~ "June",
      Month == 7 ~ "July",
      Month == 8 ~ "August",
      Month == 9 ~ "September"
    ),
    Month = fct_reorder(Month, max_temp, .desc = FALSE)
  )

# Print the result.
monthly_max_temp
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  Month     max_temp
  <fct>        <int>
1 May             81
2 June            93
3 July            92
4 August          97
5 September       93
# Visualize the maximum temperature by month.
monthly_max_temp |>
  ggplot(aes(x = max_temp, y = Month)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum Temperature by Month",
    subtitle = "Months are ordered by maximum temperature",
    x = "Maximum temperature",
    y = "Month",
    caption = "Data source: airquality dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

The chart shows that the hottest maximum temperatures happen in the summer months. This makes sense because the data covers warmer months from May through September. The ordered bar chart makes it easier to compare the months instead of reading them only in calendar order.

10 Ex 10

Using the pipe operator on the tibble air.tib, create a new column called temp_wind, which is the division of Temp by the Wind column. Investigate the relationship between Ozone amount and temp_wind by visualizing the two variables in a chart. Visualize also the associations between Wind and Ozone as well as Wind and Temp. Visualize all three sets of relationships in a single chart.

# Create temp_wind and reshape the data for faceting.
air_relationships <- air.tib |>
  mutate(
    temp_wind = Temp / Wind
  ) |>
  select(Ozone, Wind, Temp, temp_wind) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(temp_wind, Wind, Temp),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(Ozone), !is.na(value))

# Print the reshaped data to confirm it worked.
air_relationships
# A tibble: 348 × 3
   Ozone variable  value
   <int> <chr>     <dbl>
 1    41 temp_wind  9.05
 2    41 Wind       7.4 
 3    41 Temp      67   
 4    36 temp_wind  9   
 5    36 Wind       8   
 6    36 Temp      72   
 7    12 temp_wind  5.87
 8    12 Wind      12.6 
 9    12 Temp      74   
10    18 temp_wind  5.39
# ℹ 338 more rows
# Visualize the three relationships in one faceted chart.
air_relationships |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Relationships Between Ozone and Weather Variables",
    subtitle = "Comparing Ozone with temp_wind, Wind, and Temp",
    x = "Variable value",
    y = "Ozone",
    caption = "Data source: airquality dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

Based on the charts, Ozone appears to increase as temperature increases and generally decreases as wind speed increases. The temp_wind variable combines both measurements, so its relationship with Ozone looks a little stronger than either variable by itself. These are visual patterns from the data and don’t necessarily imply cause and effect.
